content.title: Rational-Number Operations, Ordering, and Absolute Value
content.overview: This lesson covers evaluating expressions involving absolute values, leading negatives, and rational number arithmetic to determine their relative order and magnitude on the number line.
learning_objectives: Define absolute value as the nonnegative distance of a number from zero.
Evaluate expressions containing absolute value signs and leading negatives.
Convert rational numbers to a common format for accurate comparison.
Order rational numbers from least to greatest or greatest to least.

sections.title: Understanding Absolute Value
sections.content: The absolute value of a number, denoted by |x|, represents its distance from zero on a number line. Because distance is never negative, the result of an absolute value operation is always a nonnegative rational number (zero or positive). For example, |-5| = 5 and |5| = 5. When an expression is inside the bars, such as |2 - 5|, you must perform the operation inside first: |2 - 5| = |-3| = 3.

sections.title: Handling Leading Negatives
sections.content: A leading negative sign outside of an absolute value bar acts as a multiplier of -1. It is applied only after the absolute value has been evaluated. For example, in the expression -| -4 |, you first evaluate |-4| to get 4, then apply the leading negative to get -4. This means -|x| will always result in a nonpositive value (zero or negative).

sections.title: Comparing and Ordering Rationals
sections.content:
To compare different rational expressions (fractions, decimals, and integers), convert them into a common form. Converting all values to decimals is often the fastest method for the ACT. Alternatively, find a common denominator for all fractions. Once in a common form, place them on a number line: values further to the right are greater, and values further to the left are smaller.

![A number line showing the relative positions of -0.75, -0.167, -0.125, and 0.25.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/a2de1d3b-c280-49c9-bd55-094dad9cb080-1786505441525-742.webp)

worked_examples.question: Which of the following values is the greatest: -| -3/4 |, | -1/2 | - 1/4, -1/8, or | -5/6 | - 1?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Evaluate absolute values. A: -(|-3/4|) = -3/4. B: (|-1/2|) - 1/4 = 1/2 - 1/4. C: -1/8. D: (|-5/6|) - 1 = 5/6 - 1. Step 2: Perform arithmetic. A = -0.75. B = 0.25. C = -0.125. D = 5/6 - 6/6 = -1/6 ≈ -0.167. Step 3: Compare the results. The values are -0.75, 0.25, -0.125, and -0.167. Since 0.25 is the only positive value, it is the greatest. Therefore, | -1/2 | - 1/4 is the greatest.

common_mistakes: Treating absolute value bars like parentheses and distributing a leading negative inside them.
Assuming that |-x| is always -x; it is always the positive version of x.
Misordering negative numbers (e.g., thinking -0.8 is greater than -0.2 because 0.8 > 0.2).
exam_tips: Always simplify the expression inside the absolute value bars before removing the bars.
Convert fractions to decimals to make comparisons faster and reduce calculation errors.
Watch for the word 'greatest' versus 'least' in the prompt to ensure you select the correct end of the number line.
content.recap: To order rational expressions, first resolve absolute values into nonnegative numbers, apply any external signs or operations, convert all results to a consistent decimal format, and then compare their positions on the number line.

knowledge_claims.content: Absolute value is defined as the nonnegative distance of a rational number from zero on the number line.
The result of an absolute value operation |x| is always greater than or equal to zero.
When evaluating -|x|, the absolute value must be resolved to a nonnegative number before the leading negative is applied.
Operations inside absolute value bars, such as |a - b|, must be completed before the absolute value is removed.
To compare rational numbers effectively, convert all values to a common form, such as decimals or fractions with a common denominator.
On a standard number line, a rational number is greater than another if it is located further to the right.
It is a mistake to change the sign of a leading negative to positive just because it is next to an absolute value bar.
Quickly estimating the decimal value of a fraction helps verify the relative ordering of rational numbers.
A leading negative applied to an absolute value, -|x|, results in a nonpositive rational number.
The expression |x - y| represents the distance between x and y on the number line.
Among negative rational numbers, the one with the smaller absolute value is the greater number (closer to zero).
Rational numbers include integers, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals that can be expressed as a ratio of two integers.

videoLesson.title: Compare Rational Values After Absolute Signs
videoLesson.description: Recognize each expression's distance-from-zero and the resulting nonnegative value. Sign out absolute values, apply leading negatives, then convert to a common form to compare numerically.
